title: From Empty Land to a Compute Beast in 90 Days! SpaceX Pours $24 Billion to Build Its Own Energy Island

content_html:
At a time when global AI compute infrastructure is being choked by both a “power bottleneck” and “long construction cycles,” tech giants often need years to take a data center from blueprint to reality. Yet SpaceX is rewriting the rules of global AI infrastructure with an engineering efficiency that almost defies common sense. Recently, blogger Sawyer Merritt posted aerial photos of SpaceX’s AI supercomputing campus at StarBase in Texas on social media, triggering a strong shockwave in the tech world. What is astonishing is that less than 90 days ago, this site was still empty land; now, multiple large buildings have already risen, with some main structures and roofing work completed. This astonishing pace of progress even prompted many overseas netizens to exclaim in the comments: “That's some Chinese level of speed.”

A $24 Billion “Compute Beast”: Not Just Built Fast, but Built Deep

The StarBase data center is by no means an ordinary server room, but a top-tier AI supercomputing hub planned by SpaceX. The project covers 444 acres and has a total investment of more than $24 billion (about 160 billion RMB). At present, more than 3,000 construction jobs have been created on site, and once operational in the future, it will support more than 500 long-term high-skilled positions. Aerial details show that multiple large energy storage units have already been neatly arranged in front of the buildings. The outside world estimates that this is a Tesla Megapack energy storage system worth more than $250 million. This means SpaceX is not only rapidly building the outer shell of compute capacity, but also simultaneously solidifying the critical underlying infrastructure—such as power supply and cooling—that determines the life or death of an AI cluster.

The Core Breakthrough: Completely Cutting Dependence on the “Public Grid”

The ultimate limit of AI is power, and the fragility and capacity ceiling of the public grid are becoming the biggest hidden concern for large-model training worldwide. SpaceX’s most core strategic insight here is this: do not rely on the public grid, and achieve absolute “energy independence.” The campus has been equipped with a dedicated natural gas power plant. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued a permit in mid-November allowing the project to install 35 natural gas turbines, with a total installed capacity of up to 750 megawatts. SpaceX has made it clear that this “self-sufficient” model can both prevent its massive electricity demand from crowding out power resources for local residents and businesses, and ensure that high power-generation costs are never passed on to existing electricity users.

Industry Takeaway: The Future of AI Competition Is a Dimensional Strike of “Vertical Integration”

Overseas netizens using “Chinese speed” to describe SpaceX precisely hits the essence of this infrastructure frenzy: in top-tier technology fields, extreme engineering execution and vertical integration capability are themselves a moat that is difficult to replicate. While other companies are still scrambling to secure grid expansion quotas and burning time on lengthy approval processes, SpaceX has already compressed the construction cycle of compute infrastructure to a suffocating 90 days through a closed loop of “self-built power plant + Tesla energy storage + ultra-fast construction.” This is not only a show of muscle by SpaceX, but also a wake-up call to the entire AI industry: on the road to AGI, competing purely on algorithms and parameters is no longer enough. Whoever is first to connect the full chain of “energy acquisition–infrastructure deployment–compute release” will be able to hold real authority at the physical layer in the next round of technological explosion.
